doc.title: Winard Harper interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, October 10, 2014

title: Why bands and gigs are harder to sustain; jazz education without audiences
summary: Fewer weeklong club engagements make touring costly; jazz education pioneers built college programs but audiences were not built.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: So why is it — I guess it’s an obvious thing here, why can’t that happen now? Javon Jackson and you and other people in that generation, it’s just harder to keep a group performing.

Part of it is there’s not enough places to play, there again. Nowadays when I look at trying to book gigs and book tours — and it’s not just me, this is from talking with other guys — there was a time where you could go out and say okay, well I’m going to play this place for a week, I know I’m here Tuesday through Sunday. If I get lucky maybe I can find something on the Monday. You know what I mean? And in most of the cities you’d go and play that jazz venue for a week. Now, a lot of times if these cities have jazz venues — during the week nowadays is very — you don’t even see that that often. Sometimes not even New York. New York is kind of like that. The Vanguard you still may see a week. Very few places do you see that Tuesday through Sunday anymore. So it’s gotten a lot harder. So as a band leader when you’re trying to take a band out, nowadays I mean most places will want to hire you for the weekend. Then you’ve got to try to figure out what am I doing Monday through Thursday? Am I sitting around paying a hotel bill or am I going to pay to send everybody back and come back again. So it’s a lot tougher since you’ve got to try to find, okay, how can I fill up the week and not have so many off days. Because off days obviously you’re paying hotels or whatever. So it’s just a lot tougher. There’s less places to play and a lot of that’s because more steps need to be made to replenish the jazz audience.

It’s ironic because jazz, like in academia now, is flourishing. Every college and, you know, at least has some jazz presence. And also you can major in jazz and so forth. It doesn’t translate to the club scene.

No because some great steps and pioneers put work in on jazz education. You know, the guy who worked for 15 years or so, Dr. Billy Taylor, Joe Newman, guys like Nathan Davis, some of those pioneers fought for and helped put jazz education in place where now most of your major colleges have jazz programs, which at one time, even when I came out of high school that was rare. A lot of schools didn’t have jazz programs. But

now all these schools have jazz programs. So we’ve done a lot to bring along musicians, but we haven’t done enough to bring along people for them to play for. So that’s where we lack. We have to come up now with some thought and some ways of building and replenishing the jazz audience. Getting some people to say look, this is something worthwhile. This is something that we need to have our young people check out. We need to have them grow with.
